claim: The headline claim that '99% of podcasts don't make it past episode 10' traces, via the article's own hyperlink, not to any study or platform disclosure but to a single individual's LinkedIn post, with no dataset, sample, or methodology behind it.
stance_target: Whether the widely circulated '99% of podcasters fail/make nothing' statistic has a traceable evidentiary basis
scope_conditions: No sample, no methodology, no platform disclosed; the claim is asserted, not measured
quoted_support: Let's start with the most damning statistic: 99% of podcasts don't make it past episode 10.
region: US/global framing; not Southeast Asia specific

claim: A second widely repeated figure in this genre -- that 25 downloads in a podcast's first week places it in the top 50% of all podcasters -- traces to a Riverside.com marketing/vendor blog rather than an independent study.
stance_target: Provenance tracing of viral podcast statistics
scope_conditions: Vendor blog (Riverside, a podcast recording/hosting company with a commercial interest in podcasting's growth narrative); no independent sample given
quoted_support: if your show gets 25 downloads in its first week, you're already in the top 50% of all podcasters.

claim: The article derives an 'average annual haul of less than $80 per podcast' by dividing Patreon's total $350 million podcast payouts (2023) across all 4.6 million existing podcasts -- a denominator that includes the overwhelming majority of shows that have no Patreon presence at all, manufacturing a mean for a population never represented in the numerator.
stance_target: The article's own arithmetic is presented as a methodological warning: aggregate payout figures divided by a population that was not the actual recipient base produce a meaningless average
scope_conditions: US/global podcast market; Patreon platform only; 2023 payout figure vs 4.6 million total podcasts (a much broader population than Patreon's actual podcast userbase)
quoted_support: Patreon paid podcasters $350 million in 2023, but with 4.6 million shows competing, the average annual haul is less than $80 per podcast

claim: The article explicitly names the survivorship-bias and aggregate-vs-distribution mechanisms that cause creator income data to be systematically misread: press coverage and industry reporting highlight top-earner outliers and aggregate market totals without disaggregating who actually receives the money.
stance_target: Survivorship bias and aggregate-growth framing systematically overstate typical creator earnings
scope_conditions: General methodological critique, applied to the podcast industry but generalizable across creator-economy reporting
quoted_support: Industry publications compound the problem. They report aggregate growth -- 584 million listeners! $4.46B in ad spend! -- without disaggregating who receives that money. The implication is that growth lifts all boats, but it actually concentrates wealth at the top.

claim: The article's own unsourced tiering asserts the top 1% of podcasts earn $50K-500K+ per episode, the next 4% earn $500-5,000 per episode, and the bottom 95% earn $0-100 per episode, with 99% receiving under $100/year -- but this tiering carries no cited dataset or methodology.
scope_conditions: No source cited; presented as the article's own synthesis ('Revenue Iceberg' framing)
quoted_support: Visible Tip (1% of Shows): $50K-500K+ per episode in ad revenue... Hidden Mass (95% of Shows): $0-100 per episode, operating at significant loss

claim: The global podcast market is estimated at $3.94-4.95 billion annually with 2025 ad spend of $4.46 billion and a 2030 market projection of $17.59 billion, while the total podcast hosting industry generates an estimated $100-150 million annually from creators paying for hosting.
stance_target: Aggregate market-size figures for podcasting (context, not creator-level income)
scope_conditions: Global podcast industry; sourced to Riverside.com and podcastindustry.org, both industry/vendor sources without disclosed sampling methodology
quoted_support: the total global podcast market generates an estimated $3.94-4.95 billion annually.
